records.source_span_text:
Appendix A                ISA Quality Attributes
The operational requirements that ISA must meet and the operating environment
characteristics that ISA must accommodate drove the quality attributes that ISA possesses.
In turn, these attributes dramatically influenced the capabilities, architecture, and
interfaces of ISA. Table 6 presents the key quality attributes of ISA.


Table 6 - ISA Quality Attributes

 Quality               Definition                          Significance to ISA


 Autonomous            Not reliant on other                Because access to another platform is never
                       components in order to              guaranteed in a tactical operating environment, ISA
                       operate at full capability          follows a distributed architecture and is designed to
                                                           be self-contained and independent, with each ISA
                                                           Controller instance able to fully support local ISA-
                                                           compliant components from a sensor
                                                           interoperability perspective.


 Discoverable          Enabling the dynamic                The dynamic nature of the tactical operating
                       determination of the existence,     environment necessitates the ability to dynamically
                       availability, and capabilities of   discover available components, which can come and
                       an asset (e.g., component,          go at any point. Hence, both ISA Controllers and
                       service)                            ISA-using systems are discoverable.


 Extensible            Able to easily add and change       Since new operational needs will arise, new DoD
                       functionality                       requirements can be levied at any time, and new
                                                           technologies are constantly being developed, ISA
                                                           was designed to facilitate introduction of new
                                                           capabilities and technologies. Examples are a new
                                                           ISA service, data encoding scheme, and
                                                           authorization mechanism.


 Fault Tolerant        Able to continue operating          The need to deal with dynamic conditions caused
                       after failure has occurred          ISA to implement a distributed architecture,
                                                           entailing the placement of the same ISA
                                                           functionality on many platforms. Hence, due to
                                                           dynamic discovery, the loss of availability of any
                                                           given ISA Controller does not inherently prevent
                                                           access to ISA services and other ISA-using systems.




                                                                                                                 59
 Quality         Definition                         Significance to ISA


High            Efficiently receives, processes,   Rapid delivery of certain sensor-related
Performance     and sends information as           communications is vital, such as alerts (e.g.,
                measured by response time,         chemical detections, gunshot detections) and
                resource utilization, and          critical tasks (e.g., slewing a camera to point at
                throughput behavior                approaching enemy). Therefore, the ISA software is
                                                   fine-tuned to perform efficiently.


Interoperable   Able to communicate with           Interoperability is fundamental to ISA’s role in
                systems operating in               meeting operational requirements by enabling all
                incompatible process domains       sensor-related assets operating in different CEs to
                                                   share data/information with each other and to
                                                   submit tasks to each other. ISA leverages existing
                                                   and emerging standards, whenever standards are
                                                   available for a required purpose, which facilitates
                                                   interoperability across a wide range of systems
                                                   with minimal changes and speeds up adoption.


Reliable        Able to achieve dependable         Since the DDIL networks common in a tactical realm
                results in the face of sub-        are characterized by high packet loss and
                optimal operating conditions       corruption, ISA uses reliable protocols to
                                                   communicate data.


Resource        Optimally using critical           Because DDIL networks have limited available
Preservative    resources (e.g., network,          bandwidth (both inherently and due to congestion),
                computing, storage), balancing     ISA leverages communications technologies and
                resource cost with operational     data dissemination patterns that enable ISA to
                value                              minimize bandwidth consumption while
                                                   maximizing delivery of the data needed by soldiers.
                                                   Furthermore, since ISA will be deployed on
                                                   constrained CEs (e.g., mobile phones), ISA was
                                                   designed to consume computing resources to a
                                                   minimal extent.


Scalable        Easy handling of a                 Since the size of an ISA deployment could be very
                progressively larger workload      large (e.g., an entire brigade combat team), ISA
                (e.g., due to increases in the     leverages data dissemination patterns and employs
                number of using systems)           data reduction techniques that enable network and
                                                   communication processing load to scale well as ISA
                                                   Controllers are added and as systems become ISA
                                                   capable.




                                                                                                         60
 Quality   Definition                        Significance to ISA


Secure    Able to resist unauthorized       As a DoD product, ISA supports a high level of
          attempts at usage or behavior     security, in particular in the areas of authentication,
          modification, while still         authorization, and confidentiality.
          providing service to legitimate
          users




                                                                                                      61
records.meaning: Defines ten architecture quality attributes and explains their intended significance for ISA design.
native_rules: Table 6 separates each quality, its definition and its significance to ISA.
The qualities are Autonomous, Discoverable, Extensible, Fault Tolerant, High Performance, Interoperable, Reliable, Resource Preservative, Scalable and Secure.

The rationale connects local autonomy and discovery to distributed architecture, communication patterns to resource use/scale, and protocol/interface choices to interoperability, reliability and security.
limitations: These are source design characteristics and claims, not measurements, test outcomes, demonstrated service-level guarantees or conformance results.
Do not turn a quality label into a current component status, ready/failed classification, benchmark value or accepted DIM property without separate modeling work.
Interoperable mentions process domains but does not define one ISA component as one OS process.
The table supplies no numerical latency, throughput, capacity, reliability or security rating.

attributes.native_definition: Not reliant on other components in order to operate at full capability
attributes.significance_summary: A distributed, self-contained Controller can support local components from the sensor interoperability perspective.

attributes.native_definition: Enabling the dynamic determination of the existence, availability, and capabilities of an asset (e.g., component, service)
attributes.significance_summary: Components and Controllers can enter/leave the network and are discoverable.

attributes.native_definition: Able to easily add and change functionality
attributes.significance_summary: The design permits new services, encodings and authorization mechanisms.

attributes.native_definition: Able to continue operating after failure has occurred
attributes.significance_summary: Distributed functionality and dynamic discovery avoid a particular Controller being inherently required for all access.

attributes.native_definition: Efficiently receives, processes, and sends information as measured by response time, resource utilization, and throughput behavior
attributes.significance_summary: The source motivates efficient software behavior by time-sensitive communications and tasks.

attributes.native_definition: Able to communicate with systems operating in incompatible process domains
attributes.significance_summary: Standards and cross-computing-environment sharing/tasking are described as the interoperability approach.

attributes.native_definition: Able to achieve dependable results in the face of sub-optimal operating conditions
attributes.significance_summary: Reliable protocols are described as the response to packet loss/corruption in DDIL conditions.

attributes.native_definition: Optimally using critical resources (e.g., network, computing, storage), balancing resource cost with operational value
attributes.significance_summary: Communications/data-dissemination choices and limited computing demand address constrained resources.

attributes.native_definition: Easy handling of a progressively larger workload (e.g., due to increases in the number of using systems)
attributes.significance_summary: Data dissemination and reduction are described as ways to accommodate larger deployments.

attributes.native_definition: Able to resist unauthorized attempts at usage or behavior modification, while still providing service to legitimate users
attributes.significance_summary: The source names authentication, authorization and confidentiality as areas of intended security support.

terms.definition: An ISA capability description contained in a component’s configuration, intended to indicate support of the capability.
A task that an ISA component can perform upon request.
A complete set of declarations of the ISA capabilities supported by an ISA component.
An ISA component that interoperates with an ISA network on behalf of the set of subcomponents contained in a composition.
A component contained within an ISA composition, other than the CIC.
A service that must be available with any ISA deployment in order to reach full capability.
A property, observable, or command declared by an ISA component.
A component that complies with the ISA interface and supports the required ISA behaviors.
A collection of components that interoperates with an ISA network via a single ISA component.
A collection of core ISA services acting as a single unit to provide ISA functionality. An ISA Controller comprises a single instance of each core ISA service.
The combination of communication protocols, security technologies, data encodings, and messages defined for ISA.
An application message exchanged over the ISA interface.
A set of interconnected ISA components.
A service defined for ISA, including core and optional services.
Information that a component can publish about observations that it makes.
A service that may be available with an ISA deployment but is not guaranteed to be present.
Information that a component can report about its current status.
A self-contained collection of related capabilities and behaviors that supports a specified interface.
A component that is not an ISA component but is exposed to an ISA network (by a CIC) in a way that makes it appear to be an ISA component.

uses: All components report declared properties upon connection and periodically

uses: All components announce availability gain/loss of a virtual ISA component

attributes.native_definition: Able to easily add and change functionality

attributes.native_definition: Able to continue operating after failure has occurred
attributes.significance_summary: Distributed functionality and dynamic discovery avoid a particular Controller being inherently required for all access.

attributes.native_definition: Efficiently receives, processes, and sends information as measured by response time, resource utilization, and throughput behavior

attributes.native_definition: Able to achieve dependable results in the face of sub-optimal operating conditions

attributes.native_definition: Optimally using critical resources (e.g., network, computing, storage), balancing resource cost with operational value
attributes.significance_summary: Communications/data-dissemination choices and limited computing demand address constrained resources.

attributes.native_definition: Easy handling of a progressively larger workload (e.g., due to increases in the number of using systems)

records.title: Terminology
records.source_span_text:
1.2       Terminology

 Table 2 - Terminology


  Term                   Description


  Component              Any participant on the ISA network that produces or consumes data. A
                         component may be hardware-based (such as a sensor) or software-based
                         (such as a data processor or user interface).


  Service                A service is a component that fulfills the requirements of a particular service
                         definition.


  Core Service           A service that must be available with any ISA deployment to reach full
                         capabilities.


  Optional Service       A service that may be available with an ISA deployment but is not
                         guaranteed to be present.


  Controller             A collection of core services acting as a single unit to provide ISA
                         functionality. A Controller comprises a single instance of each core service.




                                                                                                           1
records.meaning: Participant, service, core/optional-service and Controller meanings define ISA network roles without fixing physical-device or software-process boundaries.
native_rules: A component produces or consumes network data and may be hardware-based or software-based.
A service is a component fulfilling a service definition.
Core services must be available to obtain full deployment capabilities; optional-service availability is not guaranteed.
A Controller collects one instance of each core service and acts as a unit.
limitations: Hardware-based participant wording does not mean one participant per physical device or one operating-system process.
This terminology does not convert core-service availability into proof of activation, authorization, health or deployment conformance.
Retain the distinction between SDD software architecture and the hardware-based represented participants described here.

                         component may be hardware-based (such as a sensor) or software-based
                         (such as a data processor or user interface).


  Service                A service is a component that fulfills the requirements of a particular service
                         definition.


  Core Service           A service that must be available with any ISA deployment to reach full
                         capabilities.


  Optional Service       A service that may be available with an ISA deployment but is not
                         guaranteed to be present.


  Controller             A collection of core services acting as a single unit to provide ISA
                         functionality. A Controller comprises a single instance of each core service.

records.source_span_text:
3.3     Securing Connections
ISA components shall use Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.2 to secure
connections.

The certificate issued to the component shall be used when securing connections.

The Controller shall present its certificate to the component, and the component shall
confirm that:

   1. The certificate is signed by a trusted CA within the PKI.

   2. The Common Name within the certificate matches the Universal Component
       Identifier (UCI) of the Controller.

records.title: ISA Presentation Layer
records.source_span_text:
4.0 ISA Presentation Layer
 This section defines the process to negotiate a presentation format between the component
 and a Controller.

 The ISA Presentation Layer (IPL) allows ISA components to negotiate the presentation
 format and data encoding schema to use when exchanging data. This process allows
 components to support multiple data exchange formats.

 The protocol associated with IPL specifies the process for negotiating a presentation layer
 and method for exchanging the application data. The presentation layer negotiation is
 performed first and is used to decide the format of the data being encapsulated in the
 Application Data messages. Once the IPL format has been negotiated, the component and
 Controller can begin to exchange application messages.

 IPL supports the existence of different versions of the protocol; however, ISA version 6.0
 supports only IPL version 1.
records.meaning: IPL negotiates a presentation format/data-encoding schema before carrying application messages in that agreed format.
native_rules: Presentation negotiation occurs first and determines the format of encapsulated application data.
After negotiation the component and Controller can exchange application messages.
The IPL protocol allows versions; this edition states ISA6.0 supports only IPL version1.
limitations: IPL protocol version, format-byte pair and data-model/schema-file version remain different axes.
Negotiation completion is not component registration, authorization/configuration completion or Operational state.
Keep the ICD edition statement distinct from the separately reviewed IPL3-format guide.

records.title: IPL Formats
records.source_span_text:
4.1      IPL Formats
 IPL formats are defined using a 2 byte pair. The first byte of the pair represents the Open
 Systems Interconnection (OSI) Presentation that is to be used. The second byte specifies
 which data encoding schema to use.

 ISA currently supports two presentation formats and two types of encoding formats. The
 presentation formats are Protocol Buffers and Extensible Markup Language (XML). In most
 cases, the Protocol Buffers presentation will produce smaller messages than the XML
 presentation. Descriptions of the presentation options are provided in Table 3.




                                                                                               5
 Table 3 - OSI Presentation Formats

 Presentation        Description


 Protocol Buffers    Protocol buffers is a binary-based presentation developed by Google.


                     Extensible Markup Language is a text-based presentation developed by the World
 XML
                     Wide Web Consortium (W3C).


The encoding schemas come in two forms: Long Form and Short Form. Each data model
version will have different long and short forms. In most cases, the Long Form encoding
will produce larger messages than the Short Form. Descriptions of the encoding schema
features are provided in Table 4.


Table 4 -Schema Forms

 Schema          Description


 Long Form       This schema is generally easier to use when writing code but produces larger messages.


                 This schema is generally more difficult to use when writing code but produces smaller
 Short Form
                 messages.


Table 5 provides a mapping of IPL format byte pairs to the presentation and schema used.
The name of the schema file is also provided in the table.




                                                                                                          6
 Table 5 - IPL Formats

 Byte 1     Presentation           Byte 2      Schema                             File


 0x01       Protocol Buffers 2.X   0x01-0x05   Unsupported legacy encodings


                                   0x06        ISA 6.0 Long Form encoding         ipl-1.6-6.X.Y.proto


 0x02       XML                    0x01-0x05   Unsupported legacy encodings


                                   0x06        ISA 6.0 Long Form encoding         ipl-2.6-6.X.Y.xsd


 0x03       Protocol Buffers 2.X   0x06        ISA 6.0 Short Form encoding        ipl-3.6-6.X.Y.proto
                                               Deprecated in favor of 0x03 0x07


                                   0x07        ISA 6.0 Short Form encoding        ipl-3.7-6.X.Y.proto


 0x04       XML                    0x06        ISA 6.0 Short Form encoding        ipl-4.6-6.X.Y.xsd
                                               Deprecated in favor of 0x04 0x07


                                   0x07        ISA 6.0 Short Form encoding        ipl-4.7-6.X.Y.xsd


 0x05       Custom                 0x01        ISA 6.0.10+ Java API encoding      (none)
records.meaning: The source distinguishes encoding technology, long/short schema form, concrete format-byte pair, schema filename and legacy/deprecated standing.
native_rules: IPL format identification uses two bytes; the prose assigns presentation to byte1 and schema to byte2.
Retain all nine Table5 rows, including unsupported legacy ranges, deprecated0x03/0x06 and0x04/0x06 short forms and their0x07 replacements.
Retain0x05/0x01 Custom Java API encoding for ISA6.0.10+ with no schema file.
Long/short form and Protocol Buffers/XML descriptions are the source’s qualitative characterizations.
limitations: Do not collapse each first byte into only one PB/XML classification: native long/short pairs use distinct first-byte values.
The source’s typical size/ease statements are not benchmarks or universal guarantees.
Custom presentation encoding is not catalogue extension standing, a new physical type or an implemented binding.
No schema file was fetched, compiled, executed or tested.

records.title: Presentation Negotiation
records.source_span_text:
4.2       Presentation Negotiation
Presentation negotiation is the process used between a component and Controller to
establish the IPL format for application data exchange. The negotiation begins with a
handshake, which is initialized by the client and completed by the Controller. Using the
Handshake Begin message, the client provides the formats it wishes to use, with the most
preferred format listed first. If the Controller supports one of the requested formats, it will
respond with a Handshake Complete message containing the format selected by the
Controller.




                                                                                                        7
 Figure 1 - Handshake Success




Figure 2 - Handshake Failure
records.meaning: A client offers formats in preference order and the Controller either accepts one supported format or returns an IPL error.
native_rules: Client initiates using Handshake Begin.
Offered formats are in descending preference, most preferred first.
A Controller supporting an offered format replies with Handshake Complete specifying its choice.
Figures1 and2 show successful completion and an IPL-error reply respectively.
limitations: The source does not explicitly require the Controller to choose the highest-ranked offered format.
Figures are illustrative exchanges; no actual run, physical connection layout, application authorization or registration result is established.
The failure figure does not impose automatic disconnection.

records.title: Handshake Begin Message
records.source_span_text:
4.2.1      Handshake Begin Message
Table 6 shows the format of the IPL Handshake Begin message.




                                                               8
 Table 6 - Handshake Begin Message Format

 Byte Index    Description


 0             IPL version (0x01)


 1             Message type code (0xBB)


 2-3           Byte length of presentation formats


 4             Presentation format byte 1


 5             Presentation format byte 2


 6-n           Additional presentation formats


The IPL formats specified in the Handshake Begin message are listed in order of
preference, with bytes 4-5 listing the most preferred format. Additional formats (if
available) are listed following it, continuing the order of descending preference.

The following example Handshake Begin message lists three potential IPL formats:
Protocol Buffers Short Form (0x03 0x07), Protocol Buffers Long Form (0x01 0x06), and
XML Short Form (0x04 0x07).




                                                                                       9
 Table 7 - Handshake Begin Message Example

 Byte Index    Data         Description


 1             0x01         IPL version


 2             0xBB         Message type code


 3             0x00, 0x06   Length of formats in bytes (six bytes—three formats, two bytes per format)


 4             0x03         Presentation format 1 byte 1


 5             0x07         Presentation format 1 byte 2


 6             0x01         Presentation format 2 byte 1


 7             0x06         Presentation format 2 byte 2


 8             0x04         Presentation format 3 byte 1


 9             0x07         Presentation format 3 byte 2
records.meaning: Handshake Begin encodes IPL protocol version, message type, format-list length and ordered format-byte pairs.
native_rules: Table6 supplies byte0 IPLversion0x01, byte1 type0xBB, bytes2–3 format-byte length, bytes4–5 first pair and subsequent pairs from6 onward.
The first offered pair is most preferred; later pairs continue descending preference.
The Table7 example offers0x03/0x07,0x01/0x06 and0x04/0x07, with six format bytes.
limitations: Table7 index numbering is preserved even where it conflicts with the zero-based format table.
No general endian rule is stated or inferred; the printed example byte sequence is retained.
Three example formats are not a required/default offer list and not a tested transaction.

records.title: Handshake Complete Message
records.source_span_text:
4.2.2     Handshake Complete Message
The Handshake Complete message is sent in response to a Handshake Begin message when
an acceptable format exists, specifying the format chosen. The format of the Handshake
Complete message is shown in Table 8.




                                                                                                         10
 Table 8 - Handshake Complete Message Format

 Byte Index    Description


 0             IPL version (0x01)


 1             Message type code (0xBC)


 2             Presentation format byte 1


 3             Presentation format byte 2


An example Handshake Complete message is provided in Table 9. The message
demonstrates acceptance of Protocol Buffers Short Form (0x03 0x07) as the presentation
layer format to use when exchanging Application Data messages.


Table 9 - Handshake Complete Message Example

 Byte Index    Data             Description


 0             0x01             IPL version


 1             0xBC             Message type code


 2             0x03             Presentation format 1 byte 1


 3             0x07             Presentation format 1 byte 2
records.meaning: Handshake Complete identifies the accepted format in a four-byte control message.
native_rules: It responds to Handshake Begin when an acceptable offered format exists.
Byte0 is IPLversion0x01, byte1 type0xBC and bytes2–3 identify the chosen format.
The example chooses Protocol Buffers Short Form0x03/0x07.

 Error Code    Description

 2-3

records.title: Application Data Message
records.source_span_text:
4.3.1      Application Data Message
The IPL Application Data message is actually a collection of four message types, used based
on the size of the encapsulated message. Table 14 describes the message types and the size
restrictions for each.


Table 14 - Application Data Message Types

 Message Type       Description                   Application Data Size


 0xD1               Uses a 1-byte length field    255 bytes and under


 0xD2               Uses a 2-byte length field    256 to 65,535 bytes


 0xD4               Uses a 4-byte length field    65,536 to 4,294,967,295 bytes


 0xD8               Uses an 8-byte length field   4,294,967,296 bytes and above


The Application Data message that best fits the size of the data being exchanged should be
used. The sender does not need to restrict messages to a specific Application Data message.

The majority of application data should use the D1 and D2 messages. In some special cases,
D4 and D8 may be used, but on some networks, they could cause problems because of the
large message sizes.

Table 15 provides information on the format of the different Application Data messages.




                                                                                             14
 Table 15 - Application Data Message Format

 Byte Index      Description


 0               IPL version (0x01)


 1               Message type code (0xD1, 0xD2, 0xD4, 0xD8)

 2 (0xD1)
 2-3 (0xD2)      Byte length of the application data – The length of this field is dependent on the message
 2-5 (0xD4)      type code.
 2-9 (0xD8)

 3-n (0xD1)
 4-n (0xD2)      Application data – The length of this field is always indicated by the message length field,
 6-n (0xD4)      but the starting byte is dependent on the message type code.
 10-n (0xD8)


Table 16 provides an example of an Application Data message that contains three bytes of
data.


Table 16 - Application Data Message Example

 Byte Index    Data             Description


 0             0x01             IPL version


 1             0xD1             Message type code


 2             0x03             Application data length (three bytes)


 3             0xD5             Application data byte 1


 4             0x15             Application data byte 2


 5             0xFE             Application data byte 3
records.meaning: Application-data framing chooses one of four length-field widths while leaving the encapsulated ISA application meaning to the agreed encoding and data model.
native_rules: Table14 defines0xD1/0xD2/0xD4/0xD8 with1/2/4/8-byte application-length fields and the printed size bands.
The message that best fits the application-data size should be used; a sender need not restrict itself to one variant.
The source expects most data to use D1/D2 and cautions that large D4/D8 messages can cause problems on some networks.
Length field and payload start positions depend on the message type as Table15 specifies.
The Table16 example encloses three payload bytes D5,15,FE in a D1 frame.
limitations: The length is application-data bytes, not total frame length.
Preserve the source’s D1 lower-bound and D8 upper-bound wording without manufacturing additional normative limits.
The example bytes have no assigned DMS content or validated decoding result.
No payload meaning, physical-device taxonomy, benchmark, maximum-deployment capability, endian rule or separate model row is inferred from each framing field.

records.source_span_text:
4.3.2      IPL Error Message
In some cases, when a component receives application data, it will reply with an IPL Error
message to the sender of the data. When the component that sent the application data



                                                                                                                15
 receives the IPL Error message, it may disconnect or stay connected and take corrective
action.

The possible error codes in response to an Application Data message, and reason for the
error, are provided in Table 17.


Table 17 - IPL Error Codes (Application Data)

 Error Code     Description


 0x01           The message type code is not recognized (byte 1 of the message that was sent).


 0x02           The IPL message version is not supported (byte 0 of the Application Data message).


                An agreed-upon format has not been established. The format negotiation needs to take
 0x04
                place.


                The receiver was not able to decode the encapsulated data. This error could be caused by
 0x05           incorrectly encoded information or encoding in a format that differs from the agreed-upon
                format.


The format of the IPL Error message is provided in Table 18.


Table 18 - IPL Error Message Format

 Byte Index     Description


 0              IPL version (0x01)


 1              Message type code (0x1E)


                Length of the error information in bytes. The number of bytes from index 4 until the end of
 2-3
                the message.


 4              Error code


 5..n           Additional error information, if applicable.


Table 19 provides an example message for an encapsulated data decoding error.




                                                                                                              16
 Table 19 - IPL Error Message Example, Encapsulated Data Decode Error

 Byte Index    Data            Description


 0             0x01            IPL version


 1             0x1E            Message type code


 2-3           0x00, 0x01      Length of error data (one byte)


 4             0x05            Error decoding encapsulated data




                                                                       17

Table18 repeats the error frame; Table19 illustrates a one-byte0x05 error payload.
limitations: Keep handshake and application-data error contexts distinct;0x03 occurs in the handshake table, while0x04/0x05 occur here.
A decode error may have either of the source-listed causes; it does not prove a unique root cause, command failure or physical-device fault.

records.title: ISA Controller
records.source_span_text:
5.0 ISA Controller
 The ISA Controller is a notional software component composed of three core services.
 These services are the Communication Service, Authorization Service, and Live Data
 Service.

    •   The Communication Service acts as a host, or server, of the ISA network. It accepts
        connections from other ISA components. It is also capable of connecting to other ISA
        Controllers (Communication Services) on the network.

    •   The Authorization Service acts as the security guard of the Controller. When
        necessary, this service allows and disallows actions taken by a component.

    •   The Live Data Service provides access to the current information of components.
        This information can be accessed a single time upon request or via an ongoing
        subscription. This service manages the delivery of information when the
        information meets the needs of the subscriber.

 In most cases, when the term Controller is used in this document, it is referring more
 specifically to the Communication Service.
records.meaning: The Controller is a notional software component collecting Communication, Authorization and Live Data core services, each with a distinct responsibility.
native_rules: Communication Service acts as server/host, accepts component connections and can connect to other Controllers/Communication Services.
Authorization Service allows or disallows component actions when necessary.
Live Data Service provides current information by one-time request or ongoing subscription and delivers information matching subscriber needs.
The document qualifies that in most cases its Controller wording refers specifically to Communication Service.
limitations: Do not reduce the whole three-service Controller definition to only Communication Service.
Application authorization is separate from certificate trust and transport negotiation.
No physical controller chassis, mandatory single process, full mesh, service activation, live query result or new duplicate service rows are established.

records.title: Identification (UCI)
records.source_span_text:
6.1       Identification (UCI)
Every ISA component is identified by a Universal Component Identifier (UCI). This ID is
unique to the component and corresponds to the Common Name of the certificate used
when making the OSI transport-level connection. The requirements on a UCI are as follows:

    1. The UCI shall be unique.

    2. The UCI shall be at least one character in length.

    3. The UCI shall consist only of letters, digits, hyphens, and plus signs.

Note: These are the types of characters allowed. It is not necessary to include every type.

         a. If the component possesses a certificate, the UCI of the component shall only
             consist of letters, digits, and hyphens.

         b. If the component is a virtual component, the UCI shall consist of letters, digits,
             hyphens, and plus signs. At least one plus sign must appear in the UCI as dictated
             in Section Logically Organizing Components.

    4. The UCI shall start with a letter.

    5. The UCI shall end with a letter or a digit.

records.title: Packaging and Delivering Information
records.source_span_text:
6.2       Packaging and Delivering Information
Messages are used as a high-level data structure for exchanging information in ISA. It is not
possible to send just a message, because the destination is unknown. To send a message, it
must first be placed in an Envelope as part of the body. An Envelope body may contain
several messages of different types. The header of the Envelope is used to specify the
destination component. Once the message is placed into an Envelope and an appropriate
header is attached, the Envelope can be transmitted to the Controller to which the
component is connected. There are seven types of messages, as described in Table 20.




                                                                                                 19
 Table 20 - Message Types

 Message Type      Description


 Administrative    Information about the network, such as components joining or leaving.


 Config            Information about the configuration of a component.


 Event             Information about things the component has observed.


 Registration      A request to join or leave the network.


 Request           A request for another component to execute a command.


 Response          A response to a command request.


 Status            Information a component reports about itself.

records.title: Registering with a Controller (Registration Message)
records.source_span_text:
6.3       Registering with a Controller (Registration Message)
After connecting to the ISA network with an acceptable transport (Network Transport
Protocols), and negotiating an agreed-upon IPL format, a component must register with a
Controller. Registration is performed by placing a Registration message inside an Envelope
and sending that Envelope to the Controller. The Registration message must have the
Registration operation value of Request Add. If the registration is acceptable, the Controller
will respond with a Registration message where the Registration operation is set to Added.

records.title: Exchanging Capabilities (Config Message)
records.source_span_text:
6.4       Exchanging Capabilities (Config Message)
After registering, a component must exchange capabilities with the Controller. There are
four different categories of capabilities, as described in Table 21.




                                                                                             20
 Table 21 - Capability Categories

 Message Type        Description


 Properties          Information about the component.


                     Information the component created that is not about the component, or information
 Observables
                     about the component that is generated because it has met additional criteria (Alarms).


 Commands            Actions the component can take.


 Custom Types        Data types used by the component that are not part of the standard Data Model.


The capabilities are described using the Component Capability Declaration (CCD) and
sending it as part of the Config message.

Along with the declarations of the capabilities, the current ability of the component to use
those capabilities can be provided. The abilities fall under two categories: the readiness of
the capability and the reporting of the capability. Readiness describes if the information (or
command) is ready for use. The reporting state of the capability informs the Controller if
the information will be included in the reporting messages. For example, if a property is not
reporting, the component will not include the property in its Status message.

Whenever the capabilities change, a new Config message must be generated to provide the
most up-to-date information about the current component capabilities. A change in
capabilities includes the addition of new capabilities or a change in the ready or reporting
states of a capability.

The Controller will also provide its capabilities to the component as part of this data
exchange. The Controller also has the responsibility to inform the component if the
Controller has experienced any change in capabilities.

Table21 lists Properties, Observables, Commands and Custom Types. Properties concern the component; Observables include externally generated information and component information meeting additional criteria such as alarms; Commands are actions; Custom Types are outside the standard Data Model.
Capabilities are described using the Component Capability Declaration (CCD) and sent as part of Config.
Ready state describes current ability to use information or a command; reporting state describes inclusion in reporting messages. A property with reporting disabled is omitted from Status.
When capabilities change, a new Config must provide the current information; additions and changes of ready/reporting state count as changes.
The Controller also provides its capabilities and informs the component when its own capabilities change.

records.title: Providing Self-Component Information (Status Message)
records.source_span_text:
6.5      Providing Self-Component Information (Status Message)
The current values of the properties of the component must be always be provided to the
Controller. Whenever a significant change occurs in any property, that new property value
must be sent to the Controller. This information is provided using the Status message.



                                                                                                              21
 Due to the variety in the nature of ISA components, it is not possible to give a firm
definition to “significant change.” Instead, the needs of the end-users need to be considered.
If the change is enough that a user would want to know about it, then a new Status message
should be generated.

The frequency of Status message delivery is bounded by two properties that all
components must implement:

   •   The first property is the Minimum Status Interval, which defines the minimum
       amount of time that must occur before another Status message can be sent. This
       property prevents Status messages from being delivered too frequently.

   •   The second property is the Maximum Status Interval, which defines the maximum
       amount of time that can occur before another Status message can be sent. This
       property is necessary because Status messages are used as a heartbeat message to
       make sure the component is still alive.

All components must implement Minimum Status Interval, limiting how soon another Status may be sent, and Maximum Status Interval, limiting how long before another Status must be sent.
Maximum Status Interval serves the Status heartbeat purpose; Minimum Status Interval prevents excessive reporting frequency.

records.title: Providing Observed Information (Event Message)
records.source_span_text:
6.6     Providing Observed Information (Event Message)
When a component generates information based on an external input, or when internal
information meets threshold criteria (such as in an alarm), it is considered an observation.
This information is provided using the Event message. This information includes, but is not
limited to, weather measurements, detections, temperature alerts, and data fusion results.

Every Event message must be uniquely identifiable using the event creator (UCI), time of
the event, and the event ID. It is important to note that the time field is the time at which
the event occurred, not the time the Event message was sent.

The Event Category field can be used as a general filtering criterion for the importance of
an event. The different categories and descriptions of those categories are in Table 22.




                                                                                                22
 Table 22 - Event Categories

 Category                 Description

                          An alarm event is generated when a component property has met some criteria.
 Alarm
                          Example: The internal temperature of a computer has exceeded a threshold.

                          An alert event is generated when an observation has met some additional criteria.
 Alert
                          Example: The atmospheric temperature has exceeded a threshold.

                          A detection event is generated by a component when a change in the observable
                          space occurs. Usually, the change is the presence of a new entity in the observable
 Detection                space.

                          Example: A fusion algorithm has assembled multiple inputs into a single event.

                          A measurement event is generated when an observation is made due to a regular
                          time interval or command request.
 Measurement
                          Example: A thermometer measures the atmospheric temperature every hour, or
                          the thermometer is requested to report the current temperature.


 Other                    An event that does not fit into any of the other categories.


If the observer is able to create tracks, meaning it can update the location of an observed
entity over time, the Event message should include a Battle Space Object Identifier (BSO ID)
to identify the entity.

If a correction or an update to an event is necessary, the Event Reference should be used to
refer to the previous event. The correction data should be included in the new event. If the
new event contains observables that do not appear in the old event, the new event should
be considered additional information to the previous event. If the new event observables
do appear in the old event, the new event should be considered a correction of the previous
event.

records.title: Receiving Commands
records.source_span_text:
6.7.1     Receiving Commands
Components capable of executing commands must adhere to the following rules when
executing a command, in order to provide a uniform experience to the command sender.

To simplify component development, the Controller performs permission-checking before
forwarding the command to the executing component. Because of this procedure, any
Request message received by the component contains a command that is permitted to be
executed. There may still be other reasons that the command cannot be executed, but
permission should generally not be one of the reasons. The component may conduct
additional security checks, but they are not required.

If possible, the receiving component should determine if the command can be completed by
the stale time in the Request message. If the command cannot be completed in that time,
the caller should be notified (using a Response message with the Response Code set to
Insufficient Time).

After receiving a Request message, the component must issue a Response message within
the time defined by its Minimum Status Interval property. Responses must continue to be
created at an interval between the Minimum Status Interval and the Maximum Status
Interval property until a final Response State has been reached. Each Response must have a
reference that is set to the Request ID of the command Request. The Response must be
addressed to the calling component in the To field of the Envelope Header. Table 23
provides the possible Response Codes, their descriptions, and if they are a final state.




                                                                                           24
 Table 23 - Response Codes

 Code                       Final   Description


 Busy                       Yes     The component is busy and will not execute the command.


 Command Not Available      Yes     The command is not available for execution at this time.


 Failed                     Yes     The command began execution but was unable to complete.


 In Progress                No      The command is in the process of executing.


 Invalid Args               Yes     The command has invalid arguments.


 Invalid Command            Yes     The command is not supported by the component.


                                    The caller does not have permission to execute the command on the
 Permission Denied          Yes
                                    component.


 Queued                     No      The command has been placed in a queue for future execution.


 Success                    Yes     The command execution has successfully completed.


 Insufficient Time          Yes     The command cannot be completed before the stale time.

If possible, the component should determine whether execution can finish by Request.stale; if not, it should notify the caller with Insufficient Time.
After receiving Request, the component must issue a Response within its Minimum Status Interval.
Responses must continue at intervals between Minimum Status Interval and Maximum Status Interval until a final Response state is reached.
Each Response reference must be set to the Request ID of the command Request.
Response must be addressed to the calling component in Envelope Header To.
Table23 marks Busy, Command Not Available, Failed, Invalid Args, Invalid Command, Permission Denied, Success and Insufficient Time final; In Progress and Queued are not final.

records.title: Sending Commands
records.source_span_text:
6.7.2       Sending Commands
A component may send commands to other components on the ISA network using a
Request message. The To field in the Envelope Header should contain the UCI of the
component intended to execute the command. In the Request message, the Request ID is
used to designate the unique identification of the request.

If the command must be completed by a certain time, the calling component must use the
stale time to designate the execution deadline.

6.8        Receiving Network Information (Administrative Messages)
Administrative messages are used to share information about components on the network.
Controllers may issue Administrative messages to convey the information in Table 24.


                                                                                                        25
 Table 24 - Administrative Codes

 Code                             Description


 ALARM                            Important information about the component is being reported.


                                  Bandwidth management techniques are being applied to the
 BANDWIDTH MANAGEMENT STARTED
                                  data flow of the component.


                                  Bandwidth management techniques for the component have
 BANDWIDTH MANAGEMENT STOPPED
                                  been stopped.


 DEVICE ADDED                     A component has joined the ISA network.


                                  A component is not providing information in the expected
 DEVICE NON-RESPONSIVE
                                  time.


 DEVICE REMOVED                   A component has been removed from the network.


                                  A component that was previously non-responsive is now
 DEVICE REVIVED
                                  responding correctly.


                                  The message is created for a reason other than those provided
 OTHER
                                  in this table.


                                  A component has begun to match criteria of a data
 START FOLLOWING                  subscription, and information about the component will be
                                  delivered.


 STOP FOLLOWING                   A component no longer matches criteria of a data subscription.


 SUBSCRIPTION ADDED               A data subscription has been added for the component.


 SUBSCRIPTION REMOVED             A data subscription has been removed for the component.




                                                                                                  26

records.title: Required Capabilities
records.source_span_text:
7.1       Required Capabilities
 There are certain properties and commands that must be supported by every ISA
 component. Table 25 lists the required properties, and Table 26 lists the required
 commands.


 Table 25 - Required Properties

  Property                        Description


                                  The maximum time interval that will elapse between the sending of two
  Maximum Status Interval
                                  subsequent component statuses.


                                  The minimum time interval that must occur between the sending of two
  Minimum Status Interval         subsequent component statuses. Any state changes occurring during the
                                  interval must be cached and sent during the next allowed time.




                                                                                                          27
 Table 26 - Required Commands

 Command                                    Description


 Change Maximum Status Interval             Change the maximum status interval of a component.


 Change Minimum Status Interval             Change the minimum status interval of a component.


 Get Config                                 Get the current configuration of a component.


 Get Property                               Get the current value of a property from a component.

records.title: Standard Capabilities versus Custom Capabilities
records.source_span_text:
7.2     Standard Capabilities versus Custom Capabilities
When declaring capabilities, there are two major sets of capabilities. The first is the set of
standard capabilities, which are the capabilities defined in the ISA Data Model. These are
the preferred set of capabilities to use.

If the desired capability of the component cannot be covered by one of the standard
capabilities, a custom capability may be used. In general, custom capabilities will not be as
widely understood by other components. The data structure elements may also be
expanded using custom data types but have the same usage risks as using other custom
capabilities.

While custom capabilities are an acceptable approach to expanding ISA when necessary, it
is recommended to make every effort to match functionality with the standard capabilities.

records.title: Modifiable Properties
records.source_span_text:
7.3     Modifiable Properties
Properties can be modified using commands. By executing the appropriate command, the
component will make a change to the associated property.




                                                                                                    28
 The Set Property command is a command that can be used for providing information about
a component when that component cannot discover the information itself. An example is
for a component that needs to know its position but does not have a GPS and relies on
having the information being provided. Another component can use the Set Property
command to provide the position information.

To indicate that a property can be modified, the property must be marked as mutable in the
CCD. To indicate that the property needs a value, the property needs to be set as Not Ready
in the Config ready state.

To clear a mutable property, the Clear Property command should be used. This command
must cause the ready state of the specified property to change to Not Ready.

As a reminder, properties that are not ready must also be set as Not Reporting and not
appear in Status messages.




                                                                                          29

records.title: Logically Organizing Components
records.source_span_text:
8.0 Logically Organizing Components
 If an entity comprises pieces with duplicate capabilities, it may be necessary to represent
 the entity as several components. It is possible to logically organize the components as a
 primary component with multiple virtual components.

 When taking this approach, is important that the integration software takes care to
 represent each virtual component as a proper ISA component. The integration must do the
 following:

    •   The integration shall assign a UCI to each virtual component. The UCI of the virtual
        component shall consist of the UCI of the primary component followed by the plus
        sign and a unique identifier for the virtual component. For example, with a primary
        component with the UCI “prime,” a virtual component could be created with the UCI
        “prime+virt.”

    •   The integration shall publish Administrative messages for each virtual component
        and notify the greater ISA network when the virtual component comes online or
        goes offline.

    •   The integration shall publish Config messages, with all correct capabilities, for each
        virtual component.

    •   The integration shall publish Status messages conforming to the ISA requirements
        for each virtual component.

    •   When appropriate, the integration shall publish Event messages conforming to the
        ISA requirements. The Event shall be from the correct primary or virtual
        component.

    •   The integration shall route any messages to the appropriate virtual component.

    •   If a Request message is destined for a virtual component, the integration shall check
        the authorization of the command before execution.

    •   The integration shall discover an appropriate Live Data Service by implementing the
        Set Live Data Service command.


                                                                                               30
 •   The integration shall provide Administrative, Config, Status, and Event messages for
    its virtual components to the associated Live Data Service.




                                                                                       31

The integration shall publish conforming Status for each virtual component.
When appropriate, the integration shall publish conforming Events with the correct primary or virtual component as source.

native_text_by_page.3:
Executive Summary

The Integrated Sensor Architecture (ISA) is developed by the Army Program Executive
Officer for Intelligence, Electronic Warfare and Sensors (PEO IEW&S). The primary goal of
ISA is to enable systems to readily integrate into an existing network and dynamically
share data, information, and capabilities to help achieve situational awareness.

ISA is designed to make systems and their capabilities dynamically discoverable and
available to soldiers and platforms, without prior knowledge or specific integration, and
regardless of system type or ownership. This design maximizes access to useful data and
functionality, while minimizing integration complexity and lifecycle costs.

ISA is an interoperability solution designed to accomplish data, information, and capability
sharing within a tactical environment. ISA applies standards and technologies to address
the highly constrained communications, ever-changing conditions, and cybersecurity
demands that are characteristic of the tactical domain.

With the advent of the Army Common Operating Environment (COE) to eliminate the
capability shortfalls, cost overruns, and schedule delays that are common for system
acquisition, the Sensor Computing Environment (CE) was created to achieve sensor
interoperability across the Army’s tactical and enterprise realms. Specifically, Sensor CE is
defined to enable dynamic discovery of sensors, distribution of observation-related alerts,
dissemination of motion imagery, and control of sensors. Given ISA’s abilities and qualities,
ISA was chosen as the main material solution for Sensor CE.

records.title: Introduction
records.source_span_text:
1.0 Introduction
 The Integrated Sensor Architecture (ISA) provides interoperability and sharing of
 information between sensors and systems in a dynamic, tactical environment. To ensure
 the security of the network, ISA prevents unauthorized connections using a Public Key
 Infrastructure (PKI).

 This document outlines guidelines for certificate usage within the ISA PKI. In particular,
 certificates provided by the ISA PKI should be used solely for development, testing, and
 exercise purposes; when an ISA-integrated system is deployed, these certificates should be
 replaced by certificates provided by the PKI of the deploying organization. See the sections
 below for more detail on certificate usage in different situations.




                                                                                                1
records.source_locator: ISA Certificate Usage Guide 6.0r2 / 31 October 2023, §1.0 Introduction; PDF pages 7; printed pages 1

records.meaning: Scope and intended-use boundary of ISA PKI certificates: development, testing and exercises are distinguished from a deployed system using the deploying organization’s PKI.

native_rules.rule: The introduction attributes prevention of unauthorized network connections to ISA Public Key Infrastructure.
Certificates provided by ISA PKI should be used solely for development, testing and exercise purposes.
When an ISA-integrated system is deployed, those certificates should be replaced by certificates from the deploying organization’s PKI.

limitations: The architecture statement is not evidence that a particular installation prevents unauthorized connections.
No certificate fields, UCI binding, roles or DMS credential scheme are specified here.
This is the 31 October 2023 source scope, not a current certificate recommendation or DIM adoption.

2.0 ISA Security Infrastructure
 The PKI employed by ISA networks uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) for encryption and
 authentication. In order to connect ISA-compliant systems, appropriate TLS certificates
 must be created and installed. These certificates must be signed by trusted certificate
 authorities (CAs).

records.title: SDK Certificates
records.source_span_text:
3.1      SDK Certificates
 The ISA Software Development Kit (SDK) contains documentation, software, and schemas
 for use by engineers to accelerate the process of ISA integration. Each piece of SDK
 software requires a TLS certificate to connect to a network.

 Rather than including pre-configured certificates, the SDK provides tools for generating
 certificates matching the default configurations for the SDK software. These certificates are
 self-signed by certificate authorities that are also created in the process. The certificates
 generated for the SDK software configurations are intended for use only with the included
 SDK software and should not be used in client applications, exercises, or deployment.

native_rules.rule: The SDK includes documentation, software and schemas for ISA integration.
Each piece of SDK software requires a TLS certificate to connect to a network.
The SDK provides generation tools rather than preconfigured certificates; the generated certificates match default software configurations.
The guide describes these certificates as self-signed by certificate authorities also created in the process.
Certificates generated for SDK configurations are intended only for included SDK software and should not be used in client applications, exercises or deployment.

records.title: Manual Certificate Creation
records.source_span_text:
3.2.1     Manual Certificate Creation
The first option for creating project-specific certificates is to manually create a new
certificate authority and use it to sign new certificates for client applications. Certificates
created by a CA that is not trusted by the CA used to sign the SDK certificates will not, by
default, be able to connect to the SDK software. There are two solutions to allow them
interoperate with the SDK software:

   1.   Use the newly-created CA to create new certificates for the SDK software. In this
        approach, both the client applications and the SDK software will have been created
        by the same CA, so they will automatically trust each other.

   2.   Make the newly-created CA and the CA used to sign the SDK certificates trust each
        other: import the CA used to sign the SDK certificates into the trust stores for the
        ISA SDK software. In this approach, the client applications and the ISA SDK software
        will still have been created by separate CAs, but they will now trust each other.
records.source_locator: ISA Certificate Usage Guide 6.0r2 / 31 October 2023, §3.2.1 Manual Certificate Creation; PDF pages 10; printed pages 4

records.meaning: Two source-described approaches relate a newly created project CA to SDK-software certificate trust; the literal import direction and certificate-versus-software wording remain explicit.

native_rules.rule: Manually create a new CA and use it to sign certificates for client applications.
Certificates from a CA not trusted by the CA used to sign SDK certificates will not, by default, be able to connect to SDK software.
Use the newly created CA to create new certificates for SDK software; the source attributes automatic mutual trust to using the same CA.

The source says make the new and SDK-signing CAs trust each other and specifically says to import the SDK-signing CA into the trust stores of ISA SDK software; it then asserts interoperability between certificates from separate CAs.

limitations: CERT-SM-N002 preserves the import-direction ambiguity and the source wording that applications/software were created by CAs.
No reciprocal import instruction, trust-store repair, command line, file format or operationally complete trust setup is supplied by this review.
Descriptions of trust do not assert that certificate validation succeeded or that registration/task authorization followed.

3.2.2     Certificate Generation
The second option for creating project-specific certificates is to use the tools provided in
the ISA SDK. The following methods can be used to create root CAs, intermediate CAs, and
component certificates:

       PKI Wizard – A GUI application for creating one or more certificates in a step-by-
        step process.

       PKI Scripts – Scripts for quickly generating all certificates needed by the default SDK
        configuration, as well as individual CAs and certificates.

3.3      Exercise Certificates
SA networks created for the execution of a field exercise will each be configured with CAs
unique to that exercise. These exercise-specific CAs will be set to expire shortly after the
exercise and will trust only certificates that have been signed by the exercise CA.




                                                                                                  4
 Upon arrival at an ISA exercise, integrating ISA clients will be given appropriate certificates
signed by the exercise CA. These certificates should be used only for execution of the
exercise.

records.title: Deployment Certificates
records.source_span_text:
3.4     Deployment Certificates
The certificates signed by certificate authorities under the ISA PKI are intended for use only
in development, testing, and exercise environments. Certificates under this PKI are not
intended for use in deployment.

When deploying an ISA-integrated system, the Certificate Policy (CP) of the Program of
Record (POR) must be followed. ISA does not provide certificates for deployment. Instead,
the deploying authority must provide certificates compatible with the deployment
configuration

.

front_matter_review.source_text:
Executive Summary

The Integrated Sensor Architecture (ISA) is developed by the Army Program Executive
Officer for Intelligence, Electronic Warfare and Sensors (PEO IEW&S). The primary goal of
ISA is to enable systems to readily integrate into an existing network and dynamically
share data, information, and capabilities to help achieve situational awareness.

ISA is designed to make systems and their capabilities dynamically discoverable and
available to soldiers and platforms, without prior knowledge or specific integration, and
regardless of system type or ownership. This design maximizes access to useful data and
functionality, while minimizing integration complexity and lifecycle costs.

ISA is an interoperability solution designed to accomplish data, information, and capability
sharing within a tactical environment. ISA applies standards and technologies to address
the highly constrained communications, ever-changing conditions, and cybersecurity
demands that are characteristic of the tactical domain.

With the advent of the Army Common Operating Environment (COE) to eliminate the
capability shortfalls, cost overruns, and schedule delays that are common for system
acquisition, the Sensor Computing Environment (CE) was created to achieve sensor
interoperability across the Army’s tactical and enterprise realms. Specifically, Sensor CE is
defined to enable dynamic discovery of sensors, distribution of observation-related alerts,
dissemination of motion imagery, and control of sensors. Given ISA’s abilities and qualities,
ISA was chosen as the main material solution for Sensor CE.




                                                                                                iii

1.0 Introduction
 Integrated Sensor Architecture (ISA) supports multiple data formats that are used for
 network communications. The data format to use during communication is selected during
 the ISA Presentation Layer (IPL) negotiation. This document defines IPL Format 3 and
 describes the transformation that must occur to convert between the standard ISA Data
 Model and IPL Format 3.

 This document is intended for developers using IPL Format 3.

records.title: Component Capability Declaration
records.source_span_text:
2.0 Component Capability Declaration
 The Component Capability Declaration (CCD) declares the capabilities of the ISA
 component. Each declaration describes a single capability of the component. Because of the
 extensibility of the ISA Data Model, capabilities fall under two categories: standard and
 custom. Standard capabilities are those capabilities defined by ISA. Custom capabilities are
 used for capabilities not previously defined in ISA.

 The ISA Data Model and IPL Format 3 handle the two types of capabilities in different ways.

 The ISA Data Model uses the same declaration structure for declaring both standard and
 custom capabilities. These structures are Property Declaration, Observable Declaration, and
 Command Declaration. The Custom Data Declaration structure is used for all custom data.

 IPL Format 3 uses different declarations for standard and custom capabilities. For standard
 capabilities, the Standard Property Declaration, Standard Observable Declaration, and
 Standard Command Declaration enumerations are used. For custom capabilities, the Custom
 Property Declaration, Custom Observable Declaration, and Custom Command Declaration
 structures are used. In all cases, a union is used to link the Standard and Custom versions of
 each capability type. The Custom Data Declaration structure is used for all custom data.




                                                                                                2
 Table 2 - Capability Structures

 Capability                       ISA Data Model            IPL Format 3


 Standard Properties              Property Declaration      Standard Property Declaration


 Custom Properties                Property Declaration      Custom Property Declaration


 Standard Observable              Observable Declaration    Standard Observable Declaration


 Custom Observable                Observable Declaration    Custom Observable Declaration


 Standard Command                 Command Declaration       Standard Command Declaration


 Custom Command                   Command Declaration       Custom Command Declaration


 Custom Data                      Custom Data Declaration   Custom Data Declaration




                                                                                              3

Standard capabilities are ISA-defined; custom capabilities have not previously been defined in ISA.
The ISA Data Model uses Property Declaration, Observable Declaration and Command Declaration for both standard and custom capabilities; the guide names Custom Data Declaration for custom data.
Standard Property Declaration, Standard Observable Declaration and Standard Command Declaration are enumerations in IPL Format 3.
Custom Property Declaration, Custom Observable Declaration and Custom Command Declaration are structures; a union links the standard/custom forms for each capability kind.
The guide names Custom Data Declaration for custom data in both the Data Model and Format 3.

limitations: The source describes standard/custom encoding representation, not mandatory support for every standard capability or runtime readiness.
Standard/custom encoding does not by itself resolve the separate Custom/Nominated/Accepted extension-adoption process.
No enumeration codes, discriminator tag values, declaration member schema, compatibility matrix or name-conversion algorithm is supplied.

records.title: Status Message (Properties)
records.source_span_text:
3.0 Status Message (Properties)
 The Status message is used to report the component’s property values. The structure used
 for this is the Status composite type. When the property is reported in the status, it is
 necessary to report both the name of the property and the value of the property. The status
 message also supports the reporting of both Standard Properties and Custom Properties.

 In the ISA Data Model, both types of properties are reported in the same manner. The
 Status composite type contains a field called Properties, which is a list of the Name Value
 Pair (NVP) composite type. The Properties field is an NVP that holds the name of the
 Custom Property (NVP name) and the value of each property (NVP value).

 IPL Format 3 treats Standard Properties and Custom Properties differently. Standard
 Properties are optional fields within the Status composite type. The name of the field
 corresponds to the name of the property, while the type of the field corresponds to the type
 for the property. The property value is reported by setting the appropriate field in the
 Status message. The Properties field within the Status composite type is used to report
 Custom Properties. The Properties field is an NVP that holds the name of the Custom
 Property (NVP name) and the value of each property (NVP value).




                                                                                               4

native_rules.rule: Status reports component property values; a report conveys both a property name and its value and supports standard and custom properties.
The Data Model Status Properties field is described as a list of Name Value Pair values for both standard and custom properties.
Standard properties are optional fields of the Format 3 Status composite; field name corresponds to property name and field type to property type; setting the field reports its value.
The Format 3 Properties field reports custom properties through NVP names and values.

4.0 Event Message (Observables)
 The Event message is used to publish the component’s observations. The structure used for
 this is the Event composite type. When the observable is reported in the event, it is
 necessary to report both the name of the observable and the value of the observable. The
 event message also supports the reporting of both Standard Observables and Custom
 Observables.

 In the ISA Data Model, both types of observables are published in the same manner. The
 Event composite type contains a field called Observables, which is a list of the NVP
 composite type. The Observables field is an NVP that holds the name of the Custom
 Observable (NVP name) and the value of each observable (NVP value).

 IPL Format 3 treats Standard Observables and Custom Observables differently. Standard
 Observables are optional fields within the Event composite type. The name of the field
 corresponds to the name of the observable, while the type of the field corresponds to the
 type for the observable. The observable value is published by setting the appropriate field
 in the Event message. The Observables field within the Event composite type is used to
 report Custom Observables. The Observables field is an NVP that holds the name of the
 Custom Observable (NVP name) and the value of each observable (NVP value).
